qs.q:
UNIT 10: ECOTOURISM — NGỮ PHÁP & TỪ VỰNG (ĐỀ 1): Mark the letter A, B, C, or D on your answer sheet to indicate the correct answer to each of the following questions.
If tourists ______ rubbish on the beach, the marine ecosystem will be seriously polluted.
qs.ex: Câu điều kiện loại 1 (mệnh đề chính có 'will be') → mệnh đề If chia Hiện tại đơn: leave.

qs.q: If I ______ more free time this summer, I would join an eco-tour to Phong Nha – Ke Bang National Park.
qs.ex: Câu điều kiện loại 2 giả định trái với hiện tại (mệnh đề chính có 'would join') → mệnh đề If chia Quá khứ đơn: had.

qs.q: What would you do if you ______ a rare sea turtle laying eggs on the sand?
qs.ex: Câu điều kiện loại 2 ('What would you do if...') → mệnh đề If chia Quá khứ đơn: saw.

qs.q: If visitors touch the stalactites in the cave, the natural rock formations ______ stop growing.
qs.ex: Câu điều kiện loại 1 (mệnh đề If chia hiện tại đơn 'touch') → mệnh đề chính dùng 'will + V0'.

qs.q: True ______ involves travelling to natural areas, conserving the environment and improving the well-being of local people.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 10: ecotourism = du lịch sinh thái.

qs.q: If our village ______ a traditional weaving workshop, foreign tourists would buy more local handicrafts.
qs.ex: Câu điều kiện loại 2 (mệnh đề chính có 'would buy') → mệnh đề If chia Quá khứ đơn: opened.

qs.q: Tourists are advised to stay on marked ______ in the national park so that they do not trample rare plants.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 10: marked trails = đường mòn có đánh dấu.

qs.q: Unless we ______ the number of speedboats around the island, the coral reefs will be damaged.
qs.ex: Unless = If... not trong câu điều kiện loại 1 → dùng Hiện tại đơn: limit.

qs.q: Staying at a local family’s ______ allows visitors to experience authentic ethnic-minority cuisine and customs.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 10: homestay = nhà dân đón khách du lịch.

qs.q: If I ______ you, I wouldn’t buy souvenirs made from wild animal shells or coral.
qs.ex: Câu điều kiện loại 2 đưa ra lời khuyên: 'If I were you...'.

qs.q: Buying handmade brocade scarves helps local artisans ______ a living without cutting down forest trees.
qs.ex: Cụm từ Unit 10: earn/make a living = kiếm sống.

qs.q: If the weather ______ fine tomorrow morning, our tour guide will take us kayaking through the mangrove forest.
qs.ex: Câu điều kiện loại 1 → mệnh đề If chia Hiện tại đơn: is.

qs.q: Responsible travellers always ______ local customs and ask for permission before taking photos of villagers.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 10: respect local customs = tôn trọng phong tục địa phương.

qs.q: If mass tourism ______ unchecked in this small bay, there wouldn’t be enough clean water for residents.
qs.ex: Câu điều kiện loại 2 (mệnh đề chính có 'wouldn’t be') → mệnh đề If chia Quá khứ đơn: developed.

qs.q: Every eco-tour package is designed to minimise negative ______ on the natural environment.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 10: minimise negative impacts on... = giảm thiểu tác động tiêu cực lên...

**RESPONSIBLE ECOTOURISM GUIDELINES**
Right now, our school and community **(1)**______ a special campaign focused on sustainable ecotourism, respecting local culture and protecting nature, and we invite everyone to join us. Many eco-tourists and local guides regularly participate in ecotourism tours in nature reserves, where **(2)**______ a positive difference every week. Taking part in these activities helps young people learn how to educate travellers about local ecosystems and cultural traditions. Educators and families also note that **(3)**______ provide sustainable income for local villagers to conserve nature. This month, our organisers **(4)**______ practical workshops on how to practise responsible ecotourism, so please **(5)**______ the activities in your neighbourhood. Your active **(6)**______ will help build a better future for everyone!
(Adapted from Global Success – Unit 10: Ecotourism)

**Dear Alex,**
a. At school, our teachers also organise practical projects to help us educate travellers about local ecosystems and cultural traditions.
b. Thank you for your email; it was great to hear about your recent school activities.
c. At weekends, my friends and I join community groups to practise responsible ecotourism in nature reserves.
d. I’m writing to tell you about how we are learning about sustainable ecotourism, respecting local culture and protecting nature in Unit 10: Ecotourism.
e. Write back soon and tell me what your school is doing on this topic!
**Best wishes,**
qs.ex: Trình tự bức thư: Cảm ơn thư trước (b) → Nêu lý do viết thư chia sẻ chủ đề Unit (d) → Kể hoạt động ở trường (a) → Kể hoạt động cuối tuần (c) → Lời kết thư (e): b - d - a - c - e.

**PERSPECTIVES ON ECOTOURISM**
In recent years, sustainable ecotourism, respecting local culture and protecting nature has attracted growing attention from educators and researchers alike. A recent national survey reports that while over eighty per cent of eco-tourists and local guides recognise the importance of ecotourism tours, only about thirty-five per cent have <u>**damaged**</u> these practices into their daily routines in nature reserves. Even when resources are available, many people still struggle to balance their busy schedules with the need to practise responsible ecotourism.
The challenge lies not only in awareness but also in daily habits. Researchers note that active participants regularly engage in structured tasks that educate travellers about local ecosystems and cultural traditions, whereas passive observers only join occasional events once or twice a year. Consistent practice requires patience and planning, but it delivers lasting rewards. Many individuals simply repeat outdated habits they observed in the past, which prevents them from experiencing how ecotourism tours can provide sustainable income for local villagers to conserve nature.
Fortunately, attitudes are shifting rapidly. **[I]** Most respondents in the survey agreed that everyone should practise responsible ecotourism, even though many admitted spending less than two hours a week on it themselves. **[II]** Progress was strongest in communities where schools and families worked together as partners. **[III]** Groups can begin by setting clear weekly goals and giving every member a practical role in nature reserves. **[IV]** Small, steady steps like these can turn a difficult challenge into a shared habit of cooperation.
Promoting sustainable ecotourism, respecting local culture and protecting nature matters for the long-term future. Young people who see eco-tourists and local guides model positive behaviours are likely to view these practices as normal, and <u>**they**</u> will carry those values into adulthood. In this way, ecotourism tours not only educate travellers about local ecosystems and cultural traditions today but also provide sustainable income for local villagers to conserve nature for generations to come.
(Adapted from Educational & Social Research Reports – Unit 10: Ecotourism)

qs.ex: Trong ngữ cảnh đoạn 1, 'damaged' đồng nghĩa với 'harmed'.

**MAKING ECOTOURISM PART OF DAILY LIFE**
Taking time to practise responsible ecotourism may seem ordinary at first glance, yet a growing body of research highlights its transformative power. Studies show that well-designed ecotourism tours help eco-tourists and local guides educate travellers about local ecosystems and cultural traditions. At the same time, these practices provide sustainable income for local villagers to conserve nature and foster stronger cooperation in nature reserves.
Despite these clear advantages, participation in ecotourism tours has faced obstacles in recent years. Researchers report that <u>**they**</u> have been neglected in many busy communities due to modern time pressures. <u>**Tight timetables, heavy workloads and a lack of practical guidance can all prevent people from maintaining positive routines.**</u> Even when individuals want to improve, distractions often get in the way.
The encouraging news is that success does not require perfection from day one. Experts emphasise that building <u>**sustainable**</u> habits is about steady progress rather than instant results. Eco-tourists and local guides can start with simple steps in nature reserves, share responsibilities and use practical checklists to stay on track. Those who understand the purpose behind sustainable ecotourism, respecting local culture and protecting nature become much more resilient and motivated.
Of course, no single workshop or rule will solve every challenge overnight, and some groups need time to adapt. That is no reason to give up. Even one or two focused sessions a week can spark meaningful change, and the positive <u>**impact**</u> will grow stronger over time. What matters most is the commitment people bring to supporting one another every day.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 10: Ecotourism)

**PARTNERSHIPS BETWEEN SCHOOLS AND FAMILIES IN UNIT 10: ECOTOURISM**
Over the past two years, a research team from the National Institute of Education has tracked 1,500 high school students to evaluate how sustainable ecotourism, respecting local culture and protecting nature affects teenager development. The study found that while nearly ninety per cent of eco-tourists and local guides valued ecotourism tours, only forty-two per cent <u>**sustained**</u> these routines throughout the entire school year. Students who tried to practise alone often gave up after a few weeks when exam pressure increased.
By contrast, learners whose families and teachers coordinated their guidance achieved far more durable results. In households where parents actively joined weekend activities to practise responsible ecotourism in nature reserves, teenagers were twice as likely to educate travellers about local ecosystems and cultural traditions. Researchers explained that shared routines reduce the feeling of isolation and turn abstract classroom advice into enjoyable daily habits. Moreover, consistent family involvement helps provide sustainable income for local villagers to conserve nature without adding extra stress to students’ timetables.
Schools across the country are now redesigning their programmes based on these findings. **[I]** Instead of assigning theoretical worksheets, teachers invite parents and students to co-sign a simple weekly action plan. **[II]** This joint commitment ensures that classroom lessons are reinforced at home every evening. **[III]** At monthly review sessions, classes celebrate collective progress and exchange practical solutions to common obstacles. **[IV]**
The long-term implications of this partnership model are encouraging. When eco-tourists and local guides work side by side, <u>**they**</u> build mutual respect and lasting life skills. Ultimately, integrating sustainable ecotourism, respecting local culture and protecting nature into both school curricula and family life prepares young citizens to thrive in an increasingly complex world.
(Adapted from National Educational Research Reports – Unit 10: Ecotourism)

**WHY CONSISTENCY MATTERS MORE THAN PERFECTION IN UNIT 10: ECOTOURISM**
When people first decide to focus on sustainable ecotourism, respecting local culture and protecting nature, they often set overly ambitious targets. Enthusiastic beginners might promise to transform their entire lifestyle in a single weekend, only to feel exhausted a few days later. Studies on habit formation show that well-paced ecotourism tours are far more effective when built step by step, helping eco-tourists and local guides educate travellers about local ecosystems and cultural traditions without burnout.
The main reason crash campaigns fail is that <u>**they**</u> demand too much willpower at once. <u>**Small, consistent efforts practised every day produce far more lasting results than occasional bursts of intense activity.**</u> When a routine fits naturally into a family’s or student’s daily schedule, it requires less mental strain to maintain.
Experts therefore recommend a <u>**gradual**</u> approach to practise responsible ecotourism in nature reserves. By starting with one simple task each day and celebrating weekly milestones, learners steadily build momentum. Such steady practice not only strengthens personal discipline but also helps communities provide sustainable income for local villagers to conserve nature.
Of course, occasional setbacks are normal during busy exam weeks or family events. Rather than abandoning the goal altogether, resilient learners simply resume their routine the next morning, knowing that patience will <u>**foster**</u> long-term success.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 10: Ecotourism)

**COMMUNITY ACTION AND PEER MENTORING IN UNIT 10: ECOTOURISM**
Last year, youth unions in three provinces launched a six-month pilot programme to promote sustainable ecotourism, respecting local culture and protecting nature at the grassroots level. Instead of relying on formal lectures, organisers trained two hundred high school volunteers to lead weekend activities where neighbours could practise responsible ecotourism in nature reserves. Within the first two months, local communities reported <u>**tangible**</u> improvements in daily habits and neighbourhood solidarity.
A key factor behind this success was peer-to-peer mentoring. Teenagers often feel intimidated when adults lecture them, but they respond enthusiastically when classmates demonstrate how ecotourism tours can educate travellers about local ecosystems and cultural traditions. By working in small teams of five or six, participants shared practical tips, solved everyday problems together and helped one another provide sustainable income for local villagers to conserve nature.
Organisers also introduced simple tools to keep momentum high. **[I]** Every participating household received a visual progress board to track weekly milestones. **[II]** Local cultural centres hosted monthly gatherings where teams showcased their most creative ideas. **[III]** These celebrations turned routine tasks into a source of shared pride across the entire district. **[IV]**
Follow-up surveys conducted six months later confirmed that over seventy-five per cent of participants continued practising ecotourism tours independently. When student volunteers take ownership of community initiatives, <u>**their**</u> enthusiasm inspires both younger children and older residents. The pilot programme demonstrates that youth-led action is one of the most powerful ways to bring the values of Unit 10: Ecotourism to life.
(Adapted from Community Development & Youth Studies – Unit 10: Ecotourism)

**THE RIPPLE EFFECT OF PEER LEADERSHIP IN UNIT 10: ECOTOURISM**
How do positive habits spread across a school or neighbourhood? Sociologists studying sustainable ecotourism, respecting local culture and protecting nature have discovered that peer influence is often stronger than formal rules. When eco-tourists and local guides see their close friends willingly engage in ecotourism tours, they are far more likely to join in and educate travellers about local ecosystems and cultural traditions.
Nevertheless, launching a new initiative is never without challenges. Organisers note that initial doubts and busy routines are common, and <u>**they**</u> can slow down participation during the first week. <u>**Young people learn most effectively when they observe respected peers applying positive habits in real-life situations.**</u>
For this reason, many schools encourage <u>**voluntary**</u> student ambassadors to lead by example. Whether demonstrating how to practise responsible ecotourism in nature reserves or sharing practical tips during break time, these role models create a welcoming ripple effect that helps the whole school provide sustainable income for local villagers to conserve nature.
Even when a minor <u>**obstacle**</u> arises, a supportive peer group keeps members motivated. What begins as the effort of a few enthusiastic students soon grows into a proud tradition shared by the entire community.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 10: Ecotourism)

**Read the passage and mark the letter A, B, C or D on your answer sheet to indicate the best answer to each of the following questions from 17 to 26.**

**OVERCOMING BARRIERS TO DAILY PRACTICE IN UNIT 10: ECOTOURISM**
Why do many high school students agree that sustainable ecotourism, respecting local culture and protecting nature is important, yet still find it difficult to practise responsible ecotourism in nature reserves every day? Educational psychologists point out that modern teenagers face three main barriers: digital distractions, academic pressure and a lack of structured routines. When students feel overwhelmed, they often become <u>**reluctant**</u> to take on new responsibilities at home or in the community.
Fortunately, behavioural research shows that breaking large goals into micro-habits can overcome this hesitation. Instead of trying to change everything overnight, eco-tourists and local guides can start with a fifteen-minute daily routine focused on ecotourism tours. These manageable actions quickly build confidence and help learners educate travellers about local ecosystems and cultural traditions without interfering with their homework.
Another effective strategy is using a structured weekly checklist. **[I]** When teenagers write down specific times and places for their tasks, they are three times more likely to follow through. **[II]** Sharing <u>**it**</u> with a supportive classmate or family member adds friendly accountability. **[III]** Rather than feeling pressured, students enjoy tracking their streak of completed tasks and seeing how their efforts provide sustainable income for local villagers to conserve nature. **[IV]**
Teachers who have introduced micro-habits and checklists into their lessons on Unit 10: Ecotourism report remarkable improvements in student engagement. Once young people realise that small daily choices lead to meaningful results, ecotourism tours stops feeling like a burden and becomes a natural part of who they are.
(Adapted from Adolescent Psychology & Education Review – Unit 10: Ecotourism)
qs.q: The word **<u>reluctant</u>** in paragraph 1 is closest in meaning to ______.
qs.ex: reluctant = ngần ngại, miễn cưỡng (hesitant and unwilling).

In the digital age, some commentators worry that modern technology might distract young people from sustainable ecotourism, respecting local culture and protecting nature. **EXPERIENTIAL LEARNING AND THE FUTURE OF UNIT 10: ECOTOURISM**
Across Viet Nam, forward-thinking high schools are transforming how students learn about sustainable ecotourism, respecting local culture and protecting nature. Rather than treating Unit 10: Ecotourism as a set of vocabulary items to memorise for a test, teachers are integrating experiential learning into every week of the semester. Educators agree that hands-on practice is <u>**indispensable**</u> if young people are to educate travellers about local ecosystems and cultural traditions.
In these classrooms, students work in project teams to investigate real issues and propose ways to practise responsible ecotourism in nature reserves. For instance, learners might interview local residents, design bilingual awareness posters or organise a school-wide campaign on ecotourism tours. Through these authentic tasks, eco-tourists and local guides discover how their classroom English connects directly to everyday life.
Assessment methods are evolving alongside teaching styles. **[I]** Instead of relying solely on written quizzes, schools evaluate how effectively students collaborate and apply their plans. **[II]** Each team keeps a reflective portfolio documenting the challenges they faced and how their actions helped provide sustainable income for local villagers to conserve nature. **[III]** This approach rewards creativity, persistence and genuine teamwork rather than rote memorisation. **[IV]**
Graduates of experiential programmes consistently report higher confidence when entering university and the workplace. Students <u>**who**</u> have practised solving real-world problems in high school adapt much faster to new environments. By making sustainable ecotourism, respecting local culture and protecting nature an active, lived experience, education equips the next generation with both language proficiency and civic responsibility.
(Adapted from Modern Curriculum & Pedagogy Journal – Unit 10: Ecotourism)

**SELF-REFLECTION AND LONG-TERM GROWTH IN UNIT 10: ECOTOURISM**
Practising ecotourism tours is even more rewarding when learners take a few minutes each week to reflect on their progress. Educators studying sustainable ecotourism, respecting local culture and protecting nature have found that students who keep a brief weekly journal understand their own habits much better and find it easier to educate travellers about local ecosystems and cultural traditions.
During busy weeks, people sometimes miss a planned task or make mistakes. Without reflection, <u>**they**</u> may feel discouraged and assume that their efforts have failed. <u>**Honest self-reflection allows learners to turn early mistakes into valuable lessons rather than reasons to give up.**</u>
To make reflection effective, teachers recommend asking <u>**constructive**</u> questions every Sunday evening: What went well when we tried to practise responsible ecotourism in nature reserves this week, and what small adjustment will help us improve next week?
Over time, this simple habit deepens personal <u>**commitment**</u> and helps eco-tourists and local guides provide sustainable income for local villagers to conserve nature with confidence and pride.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 10: Ecotourism)
